new_statements.rule_in_words: No source describes where word stress fell in Silla: the language survives only in Chinese-character transcription, and the one descriptive sketch opened (Nam 2012) says nothing about tone, accent or stress. What exists are reconstructions of the pre-Middle-Korean ancestor that disagree: Whitman reconstructs lexical pitch accent (low functional load) for proto-Korean; Martin/Ramsey hold that proto-Korean probably lacked distinctive accent, Ramsey positing automatic prominence on the last syllable of the stem/morpheme, with Middle Korean's H/L/rising pitch accent arising later from syllable contraction and Chinese influence. Wikipedia (second-hand) attributes to Whitman 2015 and Lee & Ramsey 2011 the same opposition (suprasegmentals like Middle Chinese tones vs. originally no phonemic tone).
new_statements.exceptions: None; all statements are reconstructive and hedged ('probably', 'it is tempting to think so').
new_statements.domain_note: Stem/morpheme level (verb stems and nouns) in reconstructed proto-Korean; nothing at the phrase level; no citation-form data can exist for an extinct, transcription-only language.
new_statements.identity_note: sill1240 'Silla' = the Old Korean of the Silla kingdom (Glottolog: Unclassifiable, extinct, no ISO code, no descriptive references). It is the attested ancestor of Middle Korean (kore1280 lineage); the sources opened treat it as 'Old Korean' (Nam 2012) or reconstruct its ancestor as 'proto-Korean' (Whitman 2012, Martin 1996, Ramsey 1991). Kortlandt 1993 states explicitly that Middle Korean continues the Silla language. Any statement about pitch accent therefore concerns a reconstruction, not a description of a spoken variety.

sources.note: Tertiary summary: Sino-Korean tone correspondences 'suggest that Old Korean had some form of suprasegmentals consistent with those of Middle Chinese, perhaps a tonal system similar to that of Middle Korean' (citing Whitman 2015: 432-433); 'linguists such as Ki-Moon Lee and S. Roberts Ramsey argue that Old Korean originally had a simpler prosody than Middle Korean' and 'originally lacked phonemic tone' (citing Lee & Ramsey 2011: 168-169, Kwon 2005, 2016).
